choices.text: Operations are what the interpreter charges for, so they map to a bill

choices.text: Seconds are a property of the machine and the day, and operations are a property of the code

choices.text: Seconds vary with the input, and the count of operations does not
choices.why: The count of operations is precisely what varies with the input.

choices.text: Seconds cannot be measured accurately enough below a millisecond
choices.why: `timeit` measures far below that, and the measurement is still machine-specific.

choices.text: O(n²)

choices.text: When the product is small — forty rows by twelve columns is four hundred and eighty operations
choices.why: Making it a dictionary costs a reader's attention and saves nothing you can measure.

prompt: The join is by a range rather than an exact key. What replaces the nested loop?

choices.text: A dict keyed by the lower bound of each range
choices.why: A dict finds exact keys, and a range does not have one.

choices.text: A set of every value in the range, built once
choices.why: That is only possible for a small discrete range and explodes otherwise.

choices.text: Sort both sides once and walk them together in a single pass
choices.why: That is what a database calls a merge join, and it is the answer when a hash lookup will not do.

choices.text: A `Counter` over both sides, compared afterwards
choices.why: A count says how many, not which ones match.

prompt: What is the question to ask about a nested loop, according to this section?

choices.text: Whether the two collections can be loaded in one query instead
choices.why: That is a different optimisation and does not address the loop.

choices.text: How big do these collections get, in production, in a year
choices.why: The number that matters is the product rather than the shape.

choices.text: Whether the inner loop can be broken out of early
choices.why: A break improves the average and not the worst case.

choices.text: Whether the profiler has named it, which is the only evidence that counts
choices.why: The profiler names what is slow today; this question is about a year from now.

prompt: Name the complexity: a dict lookup inside a loop over `n` rows.

choices.text: O(n²), since the dict is traversed once per row
choices.why: It is not traversed at all; a lookup goes straight to a position.

choices.text: O(1), since a dict lookup is constant
choices.why: Each lookup is, and there are `n` of them.

choices.text: O(n)
choices.why: The lookup does not grow with the size of the dict, so the loop is the whole cost.

choices.text: O(n log n), since the dict has to find the key
choices.why: A dict computes a position rather than searching for one.

prompt: A queue that has things pushed on one end and taken off the other. Which structure?
hint: Both ends have to be cheap.

choices.text: A `set`, since order does not matter in a queue
choices.why: Order is the whole of what a queue is.

choices.text: A list, with `append` and `pop(0)`
choices.why: `pop(0)` shifts the whole remaining list, making the drain quadratic.

choices.text: `collections.deque`
choices.why: Constant time at both ends, where a list is `O(n)` at the front.

choices.text: `heapq`, which keeps the oldest item first
choices.why: A heap keeps the smallest item first, which is a different question.

prompt: Turn a repeated search of a list into one step per row by building this first: a `______`
Which line will the profile blame in the demonstration's report?
hint: Not the one that looked worst.

choices.text: The linear search through the whole customer list
choices.why: 13.9 seconds out of 14.4. The `in` against a list, which looked worse, was 0.49.

choices.text: The pass per country over the rows, which runs three times
choices.why: Three passes over seventeen thousand rows is a rounding error here.

choices.text: The list comprehension that builds the rows, which allocates as it goes
choices.why: It measured 0.054 seconds of its own time.

choices.text: The `in` against the blocked list, which runs on every order
choices.why: It measured 0.49 seconds, and making it a set saved seven per cent.

prompt: Which change was worth 544× and which was worth 7%?
hint: One of them the profiler pointed at.

choices.text: Both were worth about the same, and together they gave 544×
choices.why: The first was seven per cent on its own.

choices.text: The dict index was worth 544×; the set was worth 7%
choices.why: The thing that looked wrong and the thing that was slow were not the same line.

choices.text: The dict index was worth 7% and the single-pass totals were worth 544×
choices.why: The totals change took sixteen milliseconds to ten.

choices.text: The set was worth 544×; the dict index was worth 7%
choices.why: It is the other way round, which is the point of doing it in that order.

prompt: `sorted(data)` on a list of a million items, then `data.sort()` on the same list. What differs?
hint: One of them gives you something back.

choices.text: `sorted` accepts a `key` and `sort` does not
choices.why: Both take `key` and `reverse`.

choices.text: `sort` is stable and `sorted` is not
choices.why: Both are stable; it is the same algorithm.

choices.text: `sort` is `O(n)` because it needs no allocation, and `sorted` is `O(n log n)`
choices.why: Both are `O(n log n)`; the allocation is a constant factor.

choices.text: `sorted` returns a new list and leaves the original alone; `sort` changes it and returns `None`
choices.why: `sorted` is the default to reach for; `sort` is for when the list is large and you do not need the original.

prompt: A loop appends to a list and the code is slow. What do you check before rewriting anything?
hint: It might not be the append.

choices.text: Where the time is actually going, with a profiler
choices.why: `append` is 19 nanoseconds, so it is almost never the thing, and the profiler will say what is.

choices.text: Whether the list should be preallocated to its final length
choices.why: Python lists over-allocate already and preallocation buys almost nothing.

choices.text: Whether the list should be a deque, since appends are what it is for
choices.why: `append` is already `O(1)` on a list; a deque changes nothing here.

choices.text: Whether a comprehension would be faster than the explicit loop
choices.why: It is somewhat faster and it is not where nine seconds went.

prompt: `x in collection` appears inside a loop over 20,000 rows. The collection has 8 items. What do you do?

choices.text: Make it a dict, so the value is available as well
choices.why: There is no value wanted here, and a dict costs what a set costs.

choices.text: Leave it — eight comparisons is cheaper than building a set
choices.why: The crossover is somewhere under about ten items for simple values.

choices.text: Make it a set, since the loop runs twenty thousand times
choices.why: The loop count does not change that eight comparisons is already cheap.

choices.text: Move the collection outside the loop, which is where the cost is
choices.why: A literal of eight items is not what is costing anything.

prompt: An `O(n²)` function is fine today at n = 200. When does it become a problem?

choices.text: It does not — `O(n²)` at 200 is fine and stays fine
choices.why: It stays fine at 200 and nothing keeps `n` at 200.

choices.text: When it is called more often, since the cost is per call
choices.why: Calling it more often multiplies a cost that is already the issue at scale.

choices.text: When the machine gets slower, which is what makes the shape visible
choices.why: Machines do not get slower; the data gets bigger.

choices.text: When `n` grows — at 200 it is 40,000 operations and at 20,000 it is 400 million
choices.why: The question to ask is how big these get in production, in a year.

prompt: Why does the lesson say to profile before changing anything?

choices.text: Because a rewrite may change the answer, and the profile proves it did not
choices.why: A profile says where the time went, not whether the output matches.

choices.text: Because the profiler's overhead makes a later measurement unreliable
choices.why: The overhead is there whenever it runs and does not persist.

choices.text: The change that looked most wrong was worth seven per cent and the profiled one five hundred times
choices.why: The thing that looks wrong and the thing that is slow are usually not the same line.

choices.text: Because a change made first cannot be measured against the original
choices.why: You can always keep the original; the objection is about which change to make.
